analogy.p: Imagine a puck sliding on a rink so smooth that there is no friction at all, with no air either. Once you hit the puck it just keeps gliding in a straight line at the same speed, and a puck sitting still stays exactly where it is until someone hits it. That is Newton's first law: with no resultant force, nothing about the motion changes. The analogy breaks down because real rinks always have a little friction and air resistance, so a real puck gradually slows; in physics we say that happens because a small resistive force exists, not because motion naturally fades.
analogy.t: Ice hockey puck on a perfect rink

bullets: **Condition:** resultant force = 0 N. This means all the forces acting are balanced, not that there are no forces at all.
**If stationary:** the object stays stationary (velocity stays 0 m/s).
**If moving:** the object keeps the same speed AND the same direction (constant velocity), so it travels in a straight line.
The law is about the **resultant** force, which is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together.
Both parts can be summarised as: **no resultant force means no change in velocity** (no acceleration).
The opposite also holds: if the velocity changes (speed and/or direction), there **must** be a non-zero resultant force.
Mark-scheme style summary: 'zero resultant force: stationary object stays stationary, moving object continues at constant velocity (steady speed in a straight line)'.
core.h: What Newton's first law actually says
core.p: **Newton's first law** is the statement of what happens to motion when the forces on an object are **balanced**. If the **resultant force** acting on an object is **zero**, then a **stationary** object **remains stationary**, and a **moving** object **continues to move at a steady speed in a straight line** (that is, at a **constant velocity**). The law is really two statements joined together, one for objects at rest and one for objects already moving, and both rely on the single condition that the resultant force is zero. It tells you the 'default' behaviour of any object: nothing needs to push something to keep it moving, and something only changes its motion if a resultant force is applied.

bullets: **Resultant force** = the single force that could replace all the forces acting on an object and have exactly the same effect.
Same direction: add. For example 30 N + 20 N, both to the right, gives a resultant of 50 N to the right.
Opposite directions: subtract. For example 30 N right and 20 N left gives 10 N to the right.
**Balanced forces:** resultant = 0 N, e.g. 40 N right and 40 N left.
**Unbalanced forces:** resultant is not zero, so the motion changes (the object accelerates).
Because force is a vector, 'zero resultant' is about both size AND direction: forces of 10 N and 10 N at 90 degrees to each other do not balance.
Forces can be **contact forces** (friction, tension, normal contact force, air resistance) or **non-contact forces** (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic).
Drawing a **free-body diagram** (the object with arrows for each force) is the first step in any Newton's law question.
core.p: A **force** is a push or pull that acts on an object due to an interaction with another object. It is a **vector quantity**, so it has both **magnitude** (size, in newtons, N) and **direction**. Usually more than one force acts on an object, so we add them as vectors to find the **resultant force**. Forces acting along the same line in the **same direction** are added; forces acting in **opposite directions** are subtracted, and the resultant points in the direction of the larger force. When two equal and opposite forces act, the resultant is zero and we say the forces are **balanced** (the object is in equilibrium).

bullets: Weight (W) acts **downwards** from the object; the normal contact force (R) acts **upwards** from the surface.
W = R, so resultant = 0, so the book stays at rest.
Add a heavier book on top: both W and R increase together by the same amount and the stack still does not move.
A person standing still, a picture hanging on a wall (tension up, weight down) and a lamp hanging from the ceiling are further examples of balanced forces on a stationary object.
A stationary object on a slope stays still only if friction balances the component of weight down the slope; if not, it slides.

An object at the **instant** it is thrown up and reaches the top of its path has zero velocity but still has a resultant force (weight), so it does not stay at rest: being momentarily at rest is not the same as having balanced forces.
core.h: Objects at rest: why nothing happens
core.p: Take a book resting on a table. The Earth pulls it down with its **weight** (a gravitational force). The table pushes up on it with a **normal contact force** (also called the reaction force). These two are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero. Newton's first law then says the book, which is stationary, **stays stationary**. If you removed the table, the upward force would disappear, the forces would become unbalanced, and the book would accelerate downwards. This shows that to be at rest, forces do not have to be absent: they just have to be **balanced**.

bullets: A car travelling at a **constant speed** in a straight line has a resultant force of zero: **driving force = total resistive force** (friction + air resistance).
If the driving force is **greater** than resistance, the car accelerates (speeds up).
If the driving force is **less** than resistance, the car decelerates (slows down).
An ice puck on smooth ice slides a long way before stopping because friction is very small, and the smaller the friction, the closer the motion is to constant velocity.
A spacecraft far from planets and with engines off moves at constant velocity as the resultant force is approximately zero.
**Constant velocity** requires BOTH constant speed AND constant direction. A car driving round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s does not have constant velocity.
Reasoning step to quote: 'the forces are balanced, so there is no resultant force, so there is no acceleration, so the velocity stays the same'.
core.h: Moving objects: the idea that motion needs no force to continue
core.p: Many students believe a force is needed to keep an object moving. Everyday experience seems to say so, because a pushed box soon stops. But the box stops because **friction** is a resultant force that slows it down, not because motion naturally dies away. Newton's first law says that if there is **no resultant force**, a moving object will carry on at the **same speed in a straight line forever**. In deep space, far from any large mass or air, a spacecraft with its engines off keeps travelling at constant velocity. On Earth we usually need a driving force, but only to cancel resistive forces such as friction and air resistance.

bullets: **Stage 1:** only weight acts at the start, so acceleration is about 9.8 m/s2 (g).
**Stage 2:** speed rises, air resistance rises, resultant force falls, acceleration falls (the gradient of the velocity-time graph decreases).
**Stage 3:** weight = air resistance, resultant = 0, acceleration = 0, constant (terminal) velocity.
**Stage 4:** parachute opens, air resistance > weight, resultant force upwards, the skydiver decelerates.
**Stage 5:** air resistance falls as speed falls until it again equals weight: a new, lower terminal velocity.
Terminal velocity does NOT mean the forces have stopped acting; it means the forces are **balanced**.
Weight does not change when the parachute opens (the mass is the same); only the air resistance changes.
The terminal velocity depends on the **shape and surface area** of the object and its weight; a streamlined diver falls faster than a spread-eagled one.
core.h: Terminal velocity as an application of the first law
core.p: A skydiver is a good example of how forces change and then balance. At the moment of jumping, the only significant force is **weight** (downwards), so the resultant force is large and the skydiver accelerates. As speed increases, **air resistance** (drag) increases. The resultant force (weight minus air resistance) shrinks, so the acceleration shrinks. Eventually air resistance **equals** weight. The forces are balanced, the resultant force is zero, and by Newton's first law the skydiver now moves at a **constant velocity** called the **terminal velocity**. Opening a parachute increases the surface area, so air resistance suddenly becomes bigger than weight, the skydiver decelerates, and then a new, lower terminal velocity is reached when the forces balance again.

bullets: Resultant force in the **direction of motion**: object speeds up.
Resultant force **opposite** to the direction of motion: object slows down.
Resultant force at an **angle** (e.g. 90 degrees) to the direction of motion: the direction changes.
Zero acceleration does NOT mean zero velocity: a car at 30 m/s with balanced forces has zero acceleration.
Zero velocity does NOT mean zero acceleration: at the top of a vertical throw the velocity is momentarily zero but the acceleration is still 9.8 m/s2 downwards.
**Link to Newton's second law:** resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = m a). The first law is this with F = 0, giving a = 0.
**Link to Newton's third law:** the forces that balance (for example weight and normal contact force) are NOT a third-law pair, because they act on the SAME object.
core.h: What happens when the resultant force is NOT zero
core.p: Newton's first law is the 'special case' of zero resultant force; the same idea explains what happens when the resultant is not zero. A non-zero resultant force changes the **velocity** of the object, and because velocity includes direction, this means the object can **speed up**, **slow down** or **change direction**. Any change in velocity is called **acceleration**. The size of the acceleration depends on the resultant force and the mass of the object, which is Newton's second law (F = m a). So the first law tells you when there is no acceleration, and the second law tells you how large the acceleration is when there is one.

bullets: **Inertia** = the tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or of uniform (constant velocity) motion.
Inertia is **not a force**, so never write 'the force of inertia'.
More **mass** means more inertia: a lorry is much harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed.

**Bus braking:** the bus slows because of the braking force, but a passenger with no force acting on them (no seat belt) keeps moving forward at the original velocity, so they appear to move forward relative to the bus.
**Bus accelerating:** passengers seem thrown backwards because their bodies tend to stay at their original velocity while the bus moves forward.
**Seat belts and head-rests** apply a force to change the passenger's velocity safely along with the vehicle.
**Tablecloth trick:** if a cloth is pulled very quickly, friction acts for such a short time that the crockery barely moves, because of its inertia.

**Higher tier link:** **inertial mass** is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object, and is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration: inertial mass = force / acceleration (m = F / a).
core.h: Inertia: the tendency to resist changes in motion
core.p: The tendency of objects to **continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion** is called **inertia**. This is why Newton's first law is often called the law of inertia. An object with a greater mass has more inertia, so it is harder to start moving, harder to stop and harder to change direction. Inertia is not a force; it is a property of matter. It explains lots of everyday effects: passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly because their bodies tend to keep moving at the old velocity while the bus slows down.

bullets: Moving in a circle at constant speed = velocity changes (direction) = acceleration = resultant force needed.
The resultant force points **towards the centre** and is perpendicular to the velocity at every point.

Examples: tension in a string (ball whirled round), gravity on the Moon orbiting the Earth, friction between tyres and road on a roundabout, the normal contact force on a car going round a banked track.
If the force stops, the object flies off along the **tangent** at its speed at that moment, by the first law.
A force perpendicular to the velocity changes direction but not speed, so speed stays constant while velocity changes.

Common error: 'a centrifugal force pushes the object outwards'. In GCSE the correct explanation is that the object tends to go straight on (inertia) and a resultant force towards the centre is what bends its path.
If speed or mass increases, a larger centripetal force is needed to keep the object on the same circle.
core.h: Circular motion and the first law
core.p: An object moving in a **circle at constant speed** is always changing direction, so its **velocity is changing** even though its speed is not. A changing velocity means acceleration, so by the first law (the converse) there **must be a resultant force**. This force acts **towards the centre of the circle** and is called the **centripetal force**. If this force suddenly vanishes, for example a string breaks, then the first law applies: there is no resultant force, so the object moves in a **straight line** at constant velocity, along the **tangent** to the circle at the point of release (not outwards along a radius and not curving round).

bullets: Friction opposes the **relative motion** of the surfaces, so it acts opposite to the direction of motion.
Air resistance depends on **speed**, **surface area** and **shape** (streamlining reduces it).
A car at a steady 70 mph: driving force = air resistance + friction in the moving parts.
A cyclist who stops pedalling slows down because friction and air resistance give a backwards resultant force.
If there were no friction at all, a puck on a flat surface would travel at constant velocity indefinitely.
Lubrication, streamlining and smooth surfaces reduce resistive forces and so reduce the driving force needed.
Increasing the speed raises air resistance, so the driving force needed to keep a constant speed rises too, and so does fuel consumption.
core.h: Friction, air resistance and why real objects slow down
core.p: On Earth almost every moving object experiences **resistive forces**, which is why a first-law situation can look unusual. **Friction** occurs when two surfaces slide across each other, and acts in the direction **opposing** the motion, converting kinetic energy to thermal energy. **Air resistance** (drag) is friction with the air or any fluid, and increases as speed increases. To keep a vehicle moving at a constant speed, the engine's driving force must exactly match these resistive forces. Without the driving force, the resultant force would be backwards and the vehicle would decelerate.

bullets: Velocity-time graph: **gradient = acceleration** (in m/s2).
Horizontal line on v-t graph: acceleration 0, resultant force 0, forces balanced.
Straight sloping line on v-t graph: constant acceleration, constant resultant force.
Curve getting flatter: acceleration and resultant force decreasing; when it becomes horizontal, terminal velocity reached.
Distance-time graph: **gradient = speed**; straight line = constant speed = balanced forces.
Flat line on a d-t graph: stationary, forces balanced.
**Area under a v-t graph** = distance travelled.
In exam answers, state both the graph feature and the force statement: 'the line is horizontal so the velocity is constant, so the resultant force is zero'.
core.h: Reading motion graphs with the first law
core.p: The first law lets you read forces from motion graphs. On a **velocity-time graph**, a **horizontal line** means constant velocity, so the resultant force is zero. A **sloping straight line** means constant acceleration, so there is a constant non-zero resultant force. A **curve that flattens** means the acceleration is decreasing, so the resultant force is decreasing and tends to zero (as in terminal velocity). On a **distance-time graph**, a straight sloping line means constant speed (zero resultant force), a flat line means stationary (also zero resultant force), and a curve means the speed is changing (resultant force present).

bullets: **Inertial mass** = force / acceleration, measured in kilograms (kg).
Same force on two objects: the one with greater mass gets the smaller acceleration.
Example: a 10 N force gives a 2 kg trolley an acceleration of 5 m/s2, and a 10 kg trolley an acceleration of 1 m/s2.
In an exam define inertial mass as 'a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object'.
Inertial mass is found experimentally by applying a known force and measuring the acceleration (see the Newton's second law required practical).
Gravitational mass (from weight) and inertial mass turn out to have the same value, but you do not need to explain why at GCSE.
Mass is a scalar measured in kg; weight is a force measured in N; do not mix them up.
core.h: Higher tier: inertial mass and the first law in context
core.p: At Higher tier you are expected to link inertia with **inertial mass**. Inertial mass measures how hard it is to change an object's velocity, and is defined as the ratio of force to acceleration: **m = F / a**. For a given force, a large inertial mass gives a small acceleration; a small inertial mass gives a large acceleration. In this sense inertial mass tells you 'how much an object resists a change in motion'. This idea fits with the first law: with zero force the acceleration is zero whatever the mass, but with a force, mass determines the size of the effect.

bullets: First law: F = 0 so a = 0 (constant velocity, including at rest).
Second law: F = m a (for a non-zero resultant force).
Third law: equal and opposite forces between two interacting objects, acting on different objects, of the same type.
Balanced forces on ONE object (first law) are different from a third-law pair (forces on TWO objects).
Weight and the normal contact force on a book: balanced forces on the book (first law) but NOT a third-law pair.
The third-law partner of 'Earth pulls the book down' is 'the book pulls the Earth up'.
Use the first law to decide IF an object accelerates and the second law to calculate by HOW MUCH.
core.p: The three laws fit together. The **first law** says that without a resultant force there is no change in velocity. The **second law** quantifies what happens when there IS a resultant force: **F = m a**, so acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass. The **third law** says that when two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal and opposite**, acting on **different** objects. Many exam questions combine them: for example, a rocket exerts a force on its exhaust gases and the gases exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket (third law), so the rocket has a resultant force and accelerates (second law); if the engines are turned off in space, it continues at constant velocity (first law).

bullets: Step 1: Identify the forces and their directions (e.g. driving force forwards, drag backwards).
Step 2: Compare sizes: equal (balanced) or one bigger (unbalanced).
Step 3: State the resultant force: zero, or the size and direction.
Step 4: Apply the law: zero resultant means stationary stays stationary / moving stays at constant velocity; non-zero means acceleration.
Step 5: Link back to the context in the question (the car, the skydiver, the passenger).
Avoid vague words like 'it just keeps going'; say 'it continues at constant velocity because the resultant force is zero'.
Use the word 'resultant' every time you talk about the overall force.
core.h: Writing first-law explanations that earn full marks
core.p: Examiners reward a clear chain of reasoning that names the forces, states whether they are balanced, links to the resultant force, and then states what happens to velocity. Use the exact phrases from the specification: 'resultant force', 'constant velocity', 'steady speed in a straight line', 'stationary object remains stationary'. Always state the direction of the forces and refer to the object concerned. For a change in motion, name the force that causes it (for example 'friction acts backwards on the box').

exam: 1 mark: state the law or a single fact, e.g. 'the resultant force is zero' or 'constant velocity'. Use the exact wording from the specification.
2 marks: usually a fact plus a reason, e.g. 'forces are balanced / resultant force is zero, so it moves at a constant speed in a straight line'.

3 to 4 marks ('Explain'): name each force and its direction, compare them (balanced or not), state the resultant, then say what happens to the velocity and why. Keep to this chain: forces, resultant, effect on motion.

6 marks (extended): for the skydiver or car journey, go through every stage in order (acceleration, terminal velocity, parachute, new terminal velocity) and describe the forces and motion at each stage. Level 3 answers describe all stages in a logical sequence with correct use of 'resultant' and 'balanced'.
Command word 'Describe' needs what happens; 'Explain' needs why, using the force argument; 'Suggest' means apply the law to an unfamiliar context.
Always use the phrase 'resultant force' not just 'force' when you mean the overall force.
Velocity-time graph tips: horizontal = zero resultant force; read gradient for acceleration (rise over run, show the triangle); area is distance.
Do not say 'the forces cancel out' without saying the resultant is zero; say 'the forces are balanced so the resultant force is zero'.
For inertia questions (e.g. seat belts) include: the vehicle slows down, but the passenger tends to keep moving forward at the same velocity (inertia) unless a force acts.
Check the units: forces in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s2, speed in m/s.

mistakes.r: A force is only needed to change velocity. At constant velocity the resultant force is zero (driving force balances resistive forces).
mistakes.w: A force is needed to keep an object moving.

mistakes.r: A stationary object can have several forces acting; they are balanced so the resultant force is zero.
mistakes.w: No movement means there are no forces acting.

mistakes.r: The forces are still acting but they are balanced: weight = air resistance, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity is constant.
mistakes.w: Terminal velocity means the object has stopped accelerating because forces have stopped.

mistakes.r: Inertia is the tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or uniform motion; it is not a force.
mistakes.w: Inertia is a force that keeps things moving.

mistakes.r: They act on the same object so they are balanced forces (first law), not a third-law pair.
mistakes.w: Weight and the normal contact force are an action-reaction pair.

mistakes.r: Its direction changes so velocity changes, so there is a resultant force towards the centre.
mistakes.w: A car going round a bend at constant speed has zero resultant force.

mistakes.r: It moves in a straight line along the tangent at constant velocity.
mistakes.w: A ball released from circular motion flies off outwards along the radius.

mistakes.r: Weight is unchanged; air resistance increases, giving a resultant force upwards.
mistakes.w: When the parachute opens the skydiver's weight decreases.

mistakes.r: Velocity needs constant speed AND constant direction.

summary: You must know Newton's first law: if the resultant force on an object is zero, a stationary object stays stationary and a moving object continues at a steady speed in a straight line (constant velocity), and that inertia is the tendency to keep this state. It matters because it lets you explain terminal velocity, car journeys, passengers in braking vehicles and circular motion in terms of balanced and unbalanced forces.

terms.d: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, a stationary object remains stationary and a moving object continues to move at a steady speed in a straight line (constant velocity).
The single force that has the same effect on an object as all the forces acting on it together.
Forces acting on an object that are equal in size and opposite in direction so that the resultant force is zero.
Forces whose resultant is not zero, which cause the object to accelerate.
The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.
A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object; the ratio of force over acceleration (m = F / a).
Velocity that does not change in either speed or direction, so the object moves at a steady speed in a straight line.
The rate of change of velocity, in m/s2; an object accelerates if its speed and/or direction changes.
The constant velocity reached by a falling object when the resistive force (air resistance) equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, W = m g, measured in newtons (N).
The force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it, acting at right angles to the surface.
A contact force between surfaces that opposes relative motion or attempted motion.
The resistive force on an object moving through air, increasing with speed and acting opposite to the direction of motion.
A quantity that has both magnitude and an associated direction, e.g. force, velocity, acceleration.
The resultant force towards the centre of a circle that keeps an object moving in a circular path.
A diagram showing a single object with arrows representing all the forces that act on it.

worked.ans: (a) 1800 N (opposite to motion). (b) Constant velocity means zero resultant force, so the resistive force equals the driving force. (c) a = 600 N / 1200 kg = 0.50 m/s2 in the direction of travel.
worked.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travels along a straight, level road at a constant speed of 25 m/s. The driving force from the engine is 1800 N. (a) State the size of the resistive force. (b) Explain your answer. (c) The driver then increases the driving force to 2400 N. Calculate the acceleration at that instant, assuming the resistive force is unchanged. [5 marks]
steps: (a) At constant speed in a straight line the velocity is constant, so the resultant force is zero.
Resultant = driving force - resistive force = 0, so resistive force = 1800 N.
(b) Newton's first law: if the resultant force is zero a moving object continues at constant velocity, so the forces are balanced.

worked.ans: Full-mark model: 'At first only weight acts so the skydiver accelerates downwards. As speed rises, air resistance rises, so the resultant force and acceleration decrease. When air resistance equals weight the forces are balanced, the resultant force is zero and the skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity. When the parachute opens, the area is larger so air resistance is greater than weight; the resultant force is upwards so the skydiver slows down. As speed decreases, air resistance decreases until it equals weight again, giving a new, lower terminal velocity.'
worked.q: Explain, in terms of forces, why a skydiver reaches a terminal velocity and why the velocity changes when the parachute is opened. [6 marks]
steps: Start: the skydiver jumps, weight acts downwards and air resistance is small, so the resultant force is downwards and the skydiver accelerates.
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force (weight minus air resistance) decreases and so does the acceleration.
Eventually air resistance equals weight: the forces are balanced, the resultant force is zero, so by Newton's first law the skydiver moves at constant (terminal) velocity.
Parachute opens: surface area increases so air resistance becomes greater than weight, giving an upward resultant force.
The skydiver decelerates; as speed falls air resistance falls.
When air resistance again equals weight the resultant force is zero and a new, lower terminal velocity is reached.

worked.ans: The bus slows because of the braking force, but the passenger has no resultant force acting on them so continues at constant velocity (12 m/s) because of their inertia, and therefore moves forward relative to the bus.
worked.q: A passenger on a bus that is travelling at 12 m/s is not wearing a seat belt. The bus brakes suddenly and the passenger moves forward off the seat. Explain why. [3 marks]
steps: The braking force acts on the bus so the bus slows down.
No (significant) force acts forward or backward on the passenger, so their resultant force is about zero.
By the first law the passenger continues at the original velocity (inertia) while the bus slows, so relative to the bus the passenger moves forwards.
